what: Build Check Part 3 (the plain read, ROC Operations Manual §14.2A): a session that saw only Pip's statements read them as a gardener would, sentence by sentence. First read of version 0.1, second read of version 0.4.

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In Canada, one rose society says the main pruning is usually done in April, or when the forsythia is in bloom where you live. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements.label: Low

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: Let the forsythia tell you when: prune your rose when the forsythia is in flower where you live.
statements.label: High

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: Look at the buds as well: prune as they begin to swell, before any leaves open.
statements.label: Moderate

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: If your rose has winter protection, take it off first, then prune.
statements.label: Moderate

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: Wait until the danger of a hard frost has passed, or the newly pruned tips may be killed.
statements.label: Moderate

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In Toronto, one Master Gardener group says the main pruning is usually in April or May, just before new growth begins and as the buds begin to swell. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in or near Toronto only
statements.label: Low

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: On the coast of British Columbia, the main pruning is done in late winter, between late February and mid-March, as the buds begin to swell. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in or near the Lower Mainland, the Fraser Valley and Victoria only
statements.label: Moderate

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In the Okanagan, one garden company says not to prune in fall, but to wait until early spring.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in or near the Okanagan only
statements.label: Low

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: I couldn't find a source that gives a month for the main pruning in Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba. A local rose society or horticultural society is the place to ask.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba only
statements.label: No source found

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: I couldn't find rose months from a source in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island or Newfoundland and Labrador. A local rose society or horticultural society is the place to ask.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland and Labrador only
statements.label: No source found

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: Give the first feed in spring, once the spring clean-up and pruning are done and new growth begins.
statements.label: High

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: Give the last feed by mid-July, so that the stems can ripen before winter. Months are only a guide.
statements.label: Moderate

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: In Toronto, one Master Gardener group says not to feed your roses after the end of July. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in or near Toronto only
statements.label: Low

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: In Barrie and Orillia, one rose society says to feed established roses when the spring clean-up is done, again before the peak of bloom in June, and a last time in mid-July. It says not to feed after July, because the rose needs to prepare for winter. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in or near Barrie and Orillia only
statements.label: Low

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: On the coast of British Columbia, two garden companies say you can feed until late summer, and one says to give no feed from September onward. The national rose society differs: it says the last feed is in mid-July. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in or near the Lower Mainland, the Fraser Valley and Victoria only
statements.label: Sources disagree

statements.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements.text: Towards the end of the season, stop deadheading (removing the faded flowers) and let the last flowers go to seed. The hips (the rose's fruit) can stay on the stems over winter.
statements.label: Moderate

statements.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements.text: One rose grower says to stop deadheading a month before the first frost is expected.
statements.label: Low

statements.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements.text: Don't prune your rose in late summer or fall; leave the main pruning until spring. The one exception is shortening very tall canes, so that winter winds don't whip them about.
statements.label: Moderate

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: Plant a bare-root rose (one sold while dormant, not actively growing) in spring: in April, or as soon as the ground has thawed and the soil can be worked. Months are only a guide.
statements.label: Moderate

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: Outside the Prairies, you can also plant a rose in fall, at any time from September to late fall. Months are only a guide.
statements.label: Moderate

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: On the Prairies, one rose society says planting in fall is not recommended.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba only
statements.label: Low

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?

statements.shown_to: Gardeners in or near Kingston only

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: Except on the coast of British Columbia, Hybrid Tea and Floribunda roses need protecting over winter.
statements.label: High

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: In fall, as you get your roses ready for winter, remove all dead leaves and clippings from the bed.
statements.label: Moderate

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: Put the winter protection on after hard frosts, once the rose is dormant and the ground is starting to freeze. Don't put it on too early.
statements.label: High

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: Take the winter protection off in spring, once the soil has thawed and a hard freeze is no longer expected.
statements.label: High

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: Take the protection off a little at a time as the ground thaws, not all at once.
statements.label: Low

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: On the coast of British Columbia, winter protection is not usually needed, apart from a mound of soil for tender kinds. If extreme cold is forecast, protect newly planted roses, and move roses in pots into a garage or other unheated space.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in or near the Lower Mainland, the Fraser Valley and Victoria only
statements.label: Moderate

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: In Ontario, winter protection goes on in November, between early and late November, once the ground is starting to freeze. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements.label: Low

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: In Georgina, one garden centre says to wait until several hard frosts have come before covering roses, because covering too soon can trap moisture and invite rot or mildew. It says to uncover them gradually, around late April or early May, once the snow has melted and daytime temperatures stay above freezing. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in or near Georgina only
statements.label: Low

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: In Quebec, one garden company says to wait for the cooler weather of November before putting on foam cones and covers, though nets, wooden frames and snow fences can go up earlier. It says to take the protection off as soon as the snow and ice allow.
statements.label: Low

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: In Alberta, one guide says to cut the canes back to about 70 cm and remove the remaining leaves, to wait until the rose is fully dormant, and then to build the mound once the ground is at least partly frozen.
statements.label: Low

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: In Alberta, one garden company says to water your roses for the winter around 15 October, and to take the cover off around the May long weekend. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements.label: Low

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: In the Okanagan, one garden company says to mound soil or compost around the base of grafted roses in late fall.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in or near the Okanagan only
statements.label: Low

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: In Barrie and Orillia, one rose society says a dormant-oil spray early in spring, and again before the winter protection goes on, will keep disease down. If you use one, follow the label and the local rules.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in or near Barrie and Orillia only
statements.label: Low

flags.sentence: Let the forsythia tell you when: prune your rose when the forsythia is in flower where you live.
flags.problem: 5: repeats the forsythia clue already in item 1; 4: forsythia not explained
flags.suggestion: Look for forsythia (a shrub with bright yellow flowers in early spring) in your area: when it is in flower, prune your rose.

flags.sentence: ...or when the forsythia is in bloom where you live.
flags.problem: 5: forsythia clue is repeated in item 2; 4: forsythia not explained
flags.suggestion: In Canada, one rose society says the main pruning is usually done in April. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.

flags.sentence: ...and a last time in mid-July. It says not to feed after July, because the rose needs to prepare for winter.
flags.problem: 5: last feed in mid-July and no feeding after July repeat items 2, 3 and 5; 6: long, report-like
flags.suggestion: In Barrie and Orillia, one rose society says to feed established roses when the spring clean-up is done and again before the peak of bloom in June. Months are only a guide.

flags.sentence: ...once the spring clean-up and pruning are done...
flags.problem: 4: spring clean-up not explained
flags.suggestion: Give the first feed in spring, once you have pruned and cleared dead leaves and clippings from the bed, and new growth begins.

flags.sentence: ...as soon as the ground has thawed and the soil can be worked.
flags.problem: 4: 'soil can be worked' not explained
flags.suggestion: ...as soon as the ground has thawed and the soil is no longer frozen or soggy enough to dig.

flags.sentence: ...bare-root grafted roses can be ordered for planting in late fall.
flags.problem: 4: grafted not explained
flags.suggestion: ...bare-root roses (a rose joined onto a different rootstock) can be ordered for planting in late fall.

flags.sentence: Outside the Prairies, you can also plant a rose in fall...
flags.problem: 4: Prairies not defined
flags.suggestion: Outside Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, you can also plant a rose in fall, at any time from September to late fall. Months are only a guide.

flags.sentence: Except on the coast of British Columbia, Hybrid Tea and Floribunda roses need protecting over winter.
flags.problem: 3: does not say how to protect; 4: Hybrid Tea and Floribunda not explained
flags.suggestion: Except on the coast of British Columbia, protect Hybrid Tea and Floribunda roses (the common bedding roses with large or clustered blooms) over winter, for example with a mound of soil over the base.

flags.sentence: Put the winter protection on after hard frosts, once the rose is dormant...
flags.problem: 4: winter protection and dormant not explained in this statement
flags.suggestion: Put on your winter protection (such as a mound of soil or a cover) after hard frosts, once the rose has stopped growing and dropped its leaves, and the ground is starting to freeze. Don't put it on too early.

flags.sentence: Take the winter protection off in spring, once the soil has thawed and a hard freeze is no longer expected.
flags.problem: 5: overlaps item 5 on removing protection
flags.suggestion: Take the winter protection off a little at a time in spring, once the soil has thawed and a hard freeze is no longer expected, not all at once.

flags.sentence: Take the protection off a little at a time as the ground thaws, not all at once.
flags.problem: 5: repeats item 4
flags.suggestion: Merge into item 4 and delete this item.

flags.sentence: In Ontario, winter protection goes on in November, between early and late November, once the ground is starting to freeze.
flags.problem: 2: 'in November, between early and late November' says nothing extra; 5: repeats item 3
flags.suggestion: In Ontario, winter protection goes on in November, once the ground is starting to freeze. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.

flags.sentence: In Georgina, one garden centre says to wait until several hard frosts have come before covering roses, because covering too soon can trap moisture and invite rot or mildew. It says to uncover them gradually, around late April or early May...
flags.problem: 5: waiting for hard frosts and uncovering gradually repeat items 3, 4 and 5; 6: long, report-like
flags.suggestion: In Georgina, one garden centre says to uncover roses around late April or early May, once the snow has melted and daytime temperatures stay above freezing. Covering too soon can trap moisture and invite rot or mildew. Months are only a guide.

flags.sentence: ...wait until the rose is fully dormant, and then to build the mound once the ground is at least partly frozen.
flags.problem: 4: dormant not explained
flags.suggestion: ...wait until the rose has stopped growing and dropped its leaves, then build the mound once the ground is at least partly frozen.

flags.sentence: ...a dormant-oil spray early in spring, and again before the winter protection goes on, will keep disease down.
flags.problem: 4: dormant-oil spray not explained
flags.suggestion: In Barrie and Orillia, one rose society says a dormant-oil spray (a light oil sprayed on bare stems while the rose is not growing) early in spring, and again before the winter protection goes on, will keep disease down. If you use one, follow the label and the local rules.

flags.sentence: ...to water your roses for the winter around 15 October...
flags.problem: 3: unclear what watering for winter means
flags.suggestion: ...to give your roses a deep watering around 15 October, before the ground freezes, and to take the cover off around the May long weekend.

result.overall: Most answers are short and usable; the main problems are unexplained terms (forsythia, Hybrid Tea, dormant, winter protection, dormant-oil spray) and repeated winter-protection timing across the sixth question's items, with the Georgina and Barrie/Orillia items reading like reports. The no-source-found items are left unflagged as intended gap notices.

after_the_second_read.answer: Kept: the bracketed explanation of bare-root was removed at the wording check because it added a fact no finding gives.
Kept: the sentence gives a range, which rule 3 allows; the suggested span "from September to late fall" was failed at the wording check because the pages give separate times.
Kept: an explanation of Hybrid Tea and Floribunda would add a description no finding gives; the app's questions are for these roses.
Kept: "in the colder parts of Canada" is what the pages support; the wording check failed a wording that reached all of Canada except the BC coast.
Kept: it is Georgina's own local advice, shown only there; the wording check passed it with the page's alternatives kept apart.
Kept: the disagreement is said as the rules require; "check your local frost dates" would add advice no source gives.
